title: Anonymity is user-facing only; the backend keeps identity and messages
context: An anonymous campus chat needs moderation, and moderation needs to know who sent what.
options: Anonymous to the operator as well
decision: Other users see only a pseudonym. The backend retains the identity mapping and message data for moderation.
rationale: The audience is one college, a known and bounded user base. The privacy bar is that other users cannot identify you, not that the operator cannot.
tradeoffs: Users must trust the operator with their identity. A retention policy and clear wording at sign-in are required.

title: Phase 1 is a single-campus anonymous chat; the dating and reveal mechanic is deferred
context: The earlier prototype reached about 400 users in its first day or two, then usage dropped off. The long-term idea is a chat-first dating app.
decision: Build anonymous 1:1 and group chat for one campus first. Revisit the reveal mechanic only with real usage data.
rationale: Retention has to be proven on the simpler product before adding a riskier one.
tradeoffs: Phase 1 has to be valuable on its own, not just a funnel to a later feature.

title: Independent services from the start, all written in Go
context: The project is both a real product and a deliberate exercise in distributed systems.
decision: Seven services: gateway, identity, matching, chat, presence, moderation, persistence-worker. Go everywhere.
rationale: Service boundaries, contracts between services and independent deployment are the things being learned; a monolith would not exercise them.
tradeoffs: More moving parts and more operational work than a monolith for a solo developer at this scale.

title: gRPC between services, with protobuf contracts managed by buf
context: Services need typed contracts that both sides agree on.
decision: All internal calls are gRPC. The .proto files under proto/ are the source of truth; buf generates Go stubs into proto/gen/go.
rationale: Typed contracts, generated clients and servers, and streaming support. buf replaces hand-written protoc invocations.
tradeoffs: Browsers cannot call gRPC directly, so the gateway has to translate HTTP and WebSocket traffic. Proto changes affect every service.

title: RabbitMQ as the message broker
context: Live delivery must not wait on the database write, so delivery and persistence need to be decoupled.
decision: RabbitMQ carries chat messages and moderation events to the persistence worker.
rationale: Simpler to operate alone than Kafka at this scale.
tradeoffs: Queue semantics rather than a replayable log.

title: Postgres is the source of truth, accessed through repository interfaces
context: The PRD asks for a persistence layer that can be swapped later.
decision: Each service reaches its store through an interface (for example AccountStore) with a Postgres implementation behind it.
rationale: Swapping the store changes one implementation, not the service. It also allows in-memory fakes in unit tests.
tradeoffs: One extra layer per store. Fakes cannot reproduce real database behaviour (see INC-0003).

title: Redis for presence, live fan-out, caches and the match queue
context: Several features need fast, short-lived shared state across service instances.
decision: Redis holds presence counters, pub/sub channels for live delivery, the invite-code cache and the match queue.
rationale: Shared in-memory state that every instance can reach; none of it is the source of truth.
tradeoffs: Redis data can be lost on restart and must be rebuildable.

title: Deploy on k3s running on VPS nodes
context: The pilot needs real Kubernetes at low cost.
decision: A small k3s cluster on one or two VPS nodes, with managed Postgres.
rationale: Standard Kubernetes at a fraction of the cost of a managed control plane.
tradeoffs: The cluster has to be operated by hand.

title: Monorepo with a Go workspace and one module per service
context: Services must build and deploy independently but share generated proto code and small packages during development.
options: One Go module for the whole repo
One module per service tied together by go.work
decision: go.work lists pkg, proto/gen/go and each service as its own module.
rationale: Each service keeps its own dependencies and build, and local imports resolve from disk without publishing or replace directives.
tradeoffs: In workspace mode Go resolves a single version of each dependency across all modules, so one module can raise the version for the others (see INC-0004).

title: Pin dependencies to versions the installed Go toolchain can build, and set GOTOOLCHAIN=local in CI
context: See INC-0001: a dependency requiring a newer Go version triggered a toolchain download that kept failing.
options: Pin to versions compatible with the installed toolchain
decision: grpc was pinned to v1.71.1 and pgx to v5.8.0. CI sets GOTOOLCHAIN=local so a version mismatch fails fast.
rationale: A clear error is better than a silent, flaky toolchain download.
tradeoffs: Pinned versions drift behind upstream and need periodic review.

title: Badge verification checks a signed OIDC ID token, not a typed email address
context: The badge gates gender-filtered matching, so it has to prove ownership of a college account.
options: Signed ID token from the identity provider
decision: VerifyBadge takes an ID token and verifies it with a generic OIDC library (go-oidc), configured with the issuer URL.
rationale: A typed email proves nothing. A signed token can be verified without handling passwords, and a generic library keeps the provider swappable.
tradeoffs: Depends on the college's identity provider allowing third-party sign-in (confirmed for KIIT in DEC-0027).

title: Schema migrations are embedded in the binary and run at startup
context: Schema changes need an ordered, recorded history that travels with the service.
decision: golang-migrate applies the .sql files embedded with go:embed when the service starts.
rationale: The container image carries its own schema history. golang-migrate takes a Postgres advisory lock, so several replicas starting together stay safe.
tradeoffs: Startup depends on the database being reachable, and a bad migration blocks startup.

title: A shared gRPC logging interceptor is the foundation for metrics and tracing
context: Every service needs one structured log line per request, and later a trace span and a duration metric at the same point.
decision: pkg/grpclog provides a unary server interceptor that logs method, status code and duration as JSON through log/slog.
rationale: The interceptor is the single place every request passes through, so tracing and metrics extend it instead of adding a second mechanism.
tradeoffs: It covers unary calls only; streaming calls need their own interceptor.

title: go get grpc@latest required a Go toolchain download that kept failing
what_happened: go get google.golang.org/grpc@latest pulled v1.83.1, which requires Go 1.25. The installed toolchain was 1.24.3, so Go tried to download go1.25.0 and the download failed repeatedly on the network. pgx's latest release had the same requirement.
impact: Builds were blocked until the dependency versions were pinned.
root_cause: Since Go 1.21 the go directive in a dependency's go.mod is a real minimum, and GOTOOLCHAIN=auto silently downloads a newer toolchain. Leftover indirect requirement lines also kept transitive versions high after the pin.
resolution: Pinned grpc to v1.71.1 and pgx to v5.8.0, lowered the leftover indirect requirements explicitly, and set GOTOOLCHAIN=local in CI.
lessons: Do not run @latest by reflex. GOTOOLCHAIN=local turns a confusing network timeout into a clear version error.

title: go build ./... from the repo root does not span workspace modules
what_happened: Running go build ./services/... from the repo root failed with 'directory prefix services does not contain modules listed in go.work'.
impact: A single root-level build or test command could not be used locally or in CI.
root_cause: The ./... pattern does not expand across a directory that is not itself a module root.
resolution: Build and test each module from its own directory. CI runs one matrix job per module.
lessons: Per-module builds match how each service is built for deployment anyway.

title: GetAccount returned Internal and leaked a database error for a malformed account ID
what_happened: Calling GetAccount with a non-UUID ID against real Postgres returned codes.Internal with the raw Postgres error text instead of NotFound.
impact: Internal database details were exposed to callers, and a client error was reported as a server error.
root_cause: Postgres rejects a malformed UUID literal (error 22P02) before the query runs. The in-memory fake store used by the unit tests could not reproduce that path.
resolution: isNotFound in the Postgres store now maps error 22P02 to ErrNotFound.
lessons: Unit tests against fakes do not cover real database behaviour. The bug was found only by running the service against real Postgres with grpcurl; integration tests are still missing.

title: The gateway is the only public entry point and uses two separate tokens
context: Browsers cannot speak gRPC, and internal services should not be reachable from outside.
decision: The gateway translates HTTP and WebSocket traffic to gRPC and is the whole trust boundary. Google's ID token is used once, for verification; the gateway's own session token is used for everything afterwards.
rationale: One place to enforce authentication and rate limits. Internal services trust the account ID the gateway passes.
tradeoffs: A flaw in the gateway exposes everything behind it.

title: Live delivery across gateway instances goes through Redis pub/sub
context: Two people in one chat can be connected to different gateway instances, and neither instance can reach the other's sockets.
options: Pin each room to one gateway instance
Redis pub/sub fan-out with a local connection registry per instance
decision: The chat service publishes to a Redis channel per room. Each gateway instance subscribes only to rooms it has local clients in.
rationale: The chat service does not need to know which instance holds a connection, and gateways can scale horizontally.
tradeoffs: Redis pub/sub does not store messages; a disconnected client misses them unless history is loaded separately.

title: Significant plan changes are discussed and agreed before anything is built
context: The project is a learning vehicle as well as a product, and the maintainer wants to take part in each decision.
decision: Design questions are settled in discussion, one at a time, with a recommendation for each. Agreed decisions are logged here before implementation starts.
rationale: Decisions made together are understood and can be defended later.
tradeoffs: Planning takes longer before the first line of code.

title: External facts are verified against official documentation before they are stated
context: See INC-0005. Budget and architecture calculations depend on pricing, limits and product behaviour being correct.
options: Verify first and cite the source
decision: No claim about an outside product or service is made without checking its current official documentation. Anything that cannot be verified is labelled unverified.
rationale: One wrong number can invalidate a budget or a design.
tradeoffs: Planning is slower, and some answers stay unverified until a source is found.

title: Keep a small, professional set of docs and remove the knowledge base
context: docs/ had grown to a 13-article knowledge base plus several design documents that nobody would read.
options: A few maintained documents plus a decision log
decision: Root: README, CONTRIBUTING, AGENTS.md, SECURITY, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, LICENSE. docs/: PRD, ARCHITECTURE, PLAN and this log. docs/kb and docs/CONCEPT.md are removed; git history keeps them. CLAUDE.md only imports AGENTS.md.
rationale: Short documents get read and stay accurate. One rules file serves every AI tool and every human contributor.
tradeoffs: Tutorial-style explanations no longer live in the repo; reasoning is captured here in shorter form.

title: Decisions and incidents are recorded in one JSONL log
context: Decisions and their reasons were scattered across prose and chat history.
options: One Markdown ADR file per decision
decision: docs/decisions.jsonl holds one JSON object per line: decisions in the style of architecture decision records, incidents as short postmortems. Interview preparation is generated from this file instead of kept separately.
rationale: Append-only, easy to query, and readable by tools. A single source avoids two files drifting apart.
tradeoffs: Long lines are awkward to read without a tool such as jq.

title: Kafka replaces RabbitMQ; Redis pub/sub stays for live delivery
context: The maintainer is learning Kafka and wants to use it here. No code depended on RabbitMQ yet, so the switch only touched docs and the local compose file.
decision: Kafka carries durable events (chat messages, moderation events) to independent consumers. Redis pub/sub remains the low-latency path to connected clients.
rationale: Learning Kafka is an explicit goal, and Kafka is built around a retained log that several consumers read independently with per-key ordering. RabbitMQ Streams offer similar semantics, so this is not a claim that RabbitMQ could not do the job.
tradeoffs: More memory and operational work than RabbitMQ. On the pilot budget it runs as a single broker, so there is no replication.

title: The project is open source from day one
context: The repository is public and other people or AI tools may contribute.
decision: Develop in the open, with contribution, security and conduct documents in place from the first PR. The license is still to be chosen.
rationale: Public code builds trust in an anonymous app, because the claim about what is stored can be checked. It is also a portfolio piece.
tradeoffs: Anyone can read how the protections work, so secrets must never be committed and the pre-launch security review matters more.

title: GitHub Flow with CI as the merge gate
context: Earlier commits went straight to main.
decision: Every change goes through a short-lived branch and a pull request. CI must pass before merge. Pull requests are squash-merged with a Conventional Commits title. Approvals are not required while there is one maintainer.
rationale: Tested, reviewable history. GitHub does not let authors approve their own pull requests, so requiring approvals would lock out a solo maintainer.
tradeoffs: Slightly more ceremony for small changes.

title: Run the pilot on Google Cloud trial credits, on Kubernetes, and build it to be portable
context: A Google Cloud free trial provides $300 of credit over 90 days, ending 2026-12-25. Unused credit expires, and resources are stopped when the trial ends.
options: k3s on VPS from the start
Google Cloud for the pilot, then migrate
decision: Deploy the pilot to Kubernetes on Google Cloud. Move off between 2026-12-15 and 2026-12-18. Everything runs inside Kubernetes and is defined as code, and no Google-only managed services are used.
rationale: Real infrastructure at no cost for the pilot. Portability turns the December move into recreate, restore and repoint.
tradeoffs: A hard deadline, and a migration to plan. Cluster layout and cost are still to be designed.

title: v1 is the usable product plus monitoring, launched by 2026-10-15
context: The earlier prototype's best data came from its launch spike, and monitoring data cannot be collected after the fact.
options: Ship first and add monitoring later
decision: Monitoring is part of v1 and is running before the first real user. Closed beta on 2026-10-13 and 14, public launch by 2026-10-15. If something has to slip, the date slips, not safety features or monitoring.
rationale: Launch-day numbers are the most valuable and are lost if nothing is recording.
tradeoffs: More work before launch on a short timeline.

title: No performance or usage number is claimed without saved evidence
context: The project doubles as a portfolio piece, and trial infrastructure disappears when the trial ends.
options: Record measured numbers with their method
decision: A number is only quoted if a dated artefact with its method is committed to the repo: a load-test result, a dashboard export or a query result.
rationale: Claims stay checkable after the infrastructure is gone.
tradeoffs: Evidence has to be exported during the pilot, not afterwards.

title: Two tiers: guests and KIIT-verified users, with guest accounts upgraded in place
context: The question was whether to restrict the app to college accounts. Options weighed were KIIT sign-in for everyone, any Google account, fully open, or two tiers.
decision: Anyone can join as a guest with a pseudonym and use group rooms and random 1:1 matching. Signing in with a KIIT account unlocks gender-filtered matching. Signing in upgrades the same account, so rooms and pseudonym carry over. Guest accounts inactive for 60 days are deleted.
rationale: Product principle: share something about yourself to use the same thing about others. Low friction to try the app, with accountability where it matters most.
tradeoffs: Guest accounts are cheap to create, so guest signup needs rate limits and a CAPTCHA. A guest who loses their browser session loses the account.

title: KIIT verification uses Google sign-in, checks the hd claim and keys accounts on sub
context: KIIT mail is hosted on Google Workspace (MX and SPF records point to Google). A test with a real KIIT account on 2026-10-02 signed in to an unpublished third-party app and returned hd=kiit.ac.in, email_verified=true and a token lifetime of 3600 seconds.
decision: Verify the Google ID token, require hd == kiit.ac.in and email_verified, and store sub as the account's identity key.
rationale: Google states that hd must be checked when restricting access to a domain and that email should not be the primary identifier. No extra provider or email service is needed.
tradeoffs: Depends on KIIT continuing to allow third-party sign-in. The test ran while the app was in Testing status and must be repeated after publishing.

title: Gender is self-declared once after verification and only an admin can change it
context: Gender-filtered matching needs a gender. Reading it from the Google profile was considered.
options: Read gender from Google's People API
Self-declared in the app, changeable any time
decision: After KIIT sign-in the user chooses male, female or prefer not to say. The choice is enforced as permanent by the server. Changes go through a request that an admin reviews. Users who prefer not to say cannot use the gender filter and are not counted in gender totals.
rationale: Gender is not in Google's ID token, and reading it needs an additional permission and API. A Google profile gender is user-editable too, so it is no more trustworthy. The real deterrent is that a ban follows the KIIT account.
tradeoffs: Relies on an admin process for corrections. Self-declared gender can be false.

title: No public admin interface in v1
context: Admin actions (reviewing reports, banning, approving gender changes) need a surface, and the code is public.
options: Admin command-line tool used from inside the cluster
decision: Admin actions run through a command-line tool that talks to the services inside the cluster. Nothing admin-related is reachable from the internet. Every admin action is recorded with who, what, when and why.
rationale: The smallest attack surface is having no admin endpoint to attack.
tradeoffs: Less convenient than a web page, and only people with cluster access can moderate.

title: The Google OAuth client lives in its own project with no billing account
context: When the trial ends, every project linked to the trial billing account is stopped.
options: OAuth client in the trial project
decision: The OAuth client is in a separate Google Cloud project (flamingo-auth) with no billing attached.
rationale: Sign-in keeps working after the trial ends and after the backend moves to another provider. Creating and using the client without billing was confirmed on 2026-10-02.
tradeoffs: One more project to manage.

title: v1 feature scope
context: The launch needs a scope small enough for the timeline and complete enough to be safe and worth returning to.
options: PRD phase 1 plus safety at launch and a reason to return
decision: Accounts (guest, KIIT sign-in, one-time gender, new-device sign-in, change pseudonym); random and gender-filtered 1:1 matching with skip; group rooms with invite codes and one default campus room; live online counts; report and block with an admin queue and bans; saved group history; privacy policy and terms; mutual 'keep chatting' to turn a random chat into a saved conversation. Out: media, typing indicators, read receipts, push notifications, group search, profiles, native apps.
rationale: Report and block cannot wait for a later phase in an anonymous app. 'Keep chatting' addresses the drop-off after day two that ended the earlier prototype.
tradeoffs: A larger v1 than the original walking skeleton.

title: Project docs had drifted from the code
what_happened: CLAUDE.md stated that every module pins grpc v1.71.1. services/identity has required v1.74.2 since commit 8dcffcc, and in workspace mode every module therefore builds against v1.74.2. Comments in ci.yml pointed to knowledge-base paths that no longer existed.
impact: No build failure, but the documented state was wrong and could have misled a dependency change.
root_cause: The current-state section was maintained by hand and never checked against the code.
resolution: Found by running go list -m in workspace mode. The rules file now states only what a command confirms. Aligning the grpc requirement across modules is still open.
lessons: Check stated facts with a command before repeating them. Workspace mode picks one version per dependency for all modules.

title: Planning claims about outside products were made from memory and several were wrong
what_happened: During planning, statements about external products were made without checking. Examples: that RabbitMQ deletes every message once read (RabbitMQ Streams keep messages and support replay), a Google ID token lifetime that the docs do not state, and that Claude Code needs a pointer file to read AGENTS.md.
impact: Budget and architecture reasoning was briefly based on unverified statements.
root_cause: No rule required checking official documentation before stating external facts.
resolution: Every earlier claim was re-checked against official documentation and corrected or retracted. DEC-0017 makes verification a standing rule.
lessons: A plausible statement is not a verified one. Cite the source or label the claim unverified.

title: Identity checks the email suffix instead of the hd claim and keys verified accounts on email
what_happened: A review against Google's documentation found two gaps in VerifyBadge: it accepts any verified email ending in the college domain, and it treats the email as the unique identity.
impact: No known misuse; badge verification is not live yet.
root_cause: The first implementation predates reading Google's guidance. Google states the hd claim must be checked when restricting access to a domain, and that email should not be the primary identifier because it can change.
resolution: Planned with the Identity changes for v1: check hd and email_verified, and store the sub claim as the identity key.
lessons: Read the provider's verification guidance before designing the check.

title: The web frontend lives in web/ and is hosted on Vercel
context: No frontend existed in the plan. The earlier prototype used a React-based frontend on Vercel calling a Go backend.
options: Serve the frontend from the cluster
decision: The frontend is a separate app in web/ at the repo root, deployed to Vercel's free Hobby plan and calling the gateway. The framework is still to be chosen.
rationale: A familiar setup at no cost, and the frontend address does not change when the backend moves. The Hobby plan is limited to non-commercial use, which fits.
tradeoffs: Cross-origin requests need configuration at the gateway. Hobby plan limits apply.

title: Use a neutral project domain, not the maintainer's personal domain
context: Google sign-in requires an HTTPS origin that is not a raw IP address, and Google's brand verification requires DNS-level proof of domain ownership. The maintainer owns a personal domain but does not want their name in the app's address.
decision: Use a domain named after the project. Order of preference: a free first-year domain from the GitHub Student Developer Pack, a domain bought at cost from Cloudflare Registrar, a free subdomain service as a last resort. The name is not chosen yet.
rationale: A domain you control gives HTTPS for frontend and backend, brand verification, and links that survive a migration.
tradeoffs: A possible renewal cost after the first year.

title: Commits and pull request descriptions carry no AI attribution
context: Claude Code adds a Co-Authored-By trailer to commits by default. The first commit of the repository and the repository-foundation commit both carried one. The maintainer does not want AI co-authorship recorded in the history.
options: Remove it from new commits only
Remove it from new commits and from the existing history
decision: No commit message or pull request description credits an AI tool. .claude/settings.json sets attribution.commit and attribution.pr to empty strings, and AGENTS.md states the rule for other tools. The existing history was rewritten on 2026-10-03 to remove the trailer from the first commit, and main was force-pushed.
rationale: The maintainer's rule for this repository. A setting enforces it for Claude Code and a written rule covers every other tool and contributor.
tradeoffs: Rewriting the first commit changed the hash of every commit. Commit hashes recorded before 2026-10-03 no longer exist on main, and any earlier clone must be re-cloned or reset.

title: The project is licensed under Apache 2.0
context: The repository was public with no license, so nobody else could legally copy, modify or distribute the code, and it was not open source in practice.
decision: License the project under the Apache License, Version 2.0. The LICENSE file holds the unmodified text from apache.org.
rationale: A permissive license that lets anyone use, change and share the code, with an explicit patent grant from contributors and a requirement to state changes. Contributions are licensed under the same terms by section 5 of the license.
tradeoffs: Others may run modified copies without publishing their changes, which AGPL 3.0 would have required. Slightly more conditions than MIT.
